games.title: Language Choice
games.description: Choose the form that makes the unit language accurate.

rounds.prompt: Which preposition completes this sentence: Jamal was proud ______ his own strength?
rounds.answer: of
rounds.explanation: Proud always takes of, so we say proud of a person, a job or an achievement.

rounds.prompt: Which word means broken pieces of stone and brick left after a building falls?
rounds.answer: rubble
rounds.explanation: Rubble is the wreckage itself. A pouch is a small bag, nutrition is the goodness in food, and a species is a group of similar living things.

rounds.prompt: In “The Camel and the Sparrow”, what did Zara see from high above the village?
choices: A lorry passing on the damaged road
A market full of busy traders
A hidden stream behind the ridge
rounds.answer: A hidden stream behind the ridge
rounds.explanation: From the sky Zara spotted a thin green line to the east, which turned out to be the stream the village needed.

rounds.prompt: What is the moral of “The Camel and the Sparrow”?
choices: Strength always wins in the end
rounds.answer: No contribution is too small
rounds.explanation: The fable ends by stating it plainly, because the smallest character found the water that saved the village.

rounds.prompt: Which sentence uses the adjective and preposition pair correctly?
choices: He was afraid from the dark corridor.
We are excited about the trip.
rounds.answer: We are excited about the trip.
rounds.explanation: Excited takes about. The other three need at, of and in instead of the prepositions shown.

rounds.prompt: What does the word urban mean?
choices: Related to a city or town
Related to the sea or ocean
rounds.answer: Related to a city or town
rounds.explanation: Urban describes city life. Its opposite, rural, describes the countryside, while marine belongs to the sea and artificial means man-made.

games.title: Reading Detective
games.description: Use unit evidence to solve each reading clue.

rounds.prompt: In “What Makes a Fable?”, what name is given to the lesson at the end of a fable?
choices: The lesson at the end of a fable is called the moral.
It names “The Tortoise and the Hare” and “The Boy Who Cried Wolf”.
It gives both animals real value, so the moral that no contribution is too small feels earned rather than sudden.
rounds.answer: The lesson at the end of a fable is called the moral.
rounds.explanation: The opening sentence states it directly: a fable teaches a lesson, and that lesson is called the moral.

rounds.prompt: Which two fables by Aesop does “Folklore Around the World” name?
choices: They all chose to teach through a short story with a lesson folded inside it.
She swept the steps and filled the water jug on the judge’s bench.
It names “The Tortoise and the Hare” and “The Boy Who Cried Wolf”.
rounds.answer: It names “The Tortoise and the Hare” and “The Boy Who Cried Wolf”.
rounds.explanation: Both titles appear in the sentence about ancient Greece, where the text calls them known almost everywhere.

rounds.prompt: In “The Camel and the Sparrow”, what did the villagers find when the misty dawn came after the sandstorm?
choices: She thinks the ground is shaking again, because an earthquake had damaged the town two years earlier.
They found their homes in rubble, with walls crumbled, roofs blown away and the well buried under sand.
They all chose to teach through a short story with a lesson folded inside it.
rounds.answer: They found their homes in rubble, with walls crumbled, roofs blown away and the well buried under sand.
rounds.explanation: The paragraph after the sandstorm lists the damage in order: crumbled walls, missing roofs, then the buried well.

rounds.prompt: Why could Zara find the hidden stream when nobody on the ground could?
choices: She flew higher than any camel could reach, so from the sky she saw the thin green line behind the ridge.
They found their homes in rubble, with walls crumbled, roofs blown away and the well buried under sand.
He said he had seen the trader hide boxes behind the artificial wall in the storehouse.
rounds.answer: She flew higher than any camel could reach, so from the sky she saw the thin green line behind the ridge.
rounds.explanation: The fable links her height to her discovery: from up there she saw what nobody on the ground could see.

rounds.prompt: In part 1 of “The Silence After the Rumble”, what two jobs did Amal do at the courthouse each morning?
choices: She feels a wave of anxiety, and the fable says she wondered whether she was simply too small to matter.
She now counts unlocking the doors as real work at the court, so she claims her role instead of shrinking it.
She swept the steps and filled the water jug on the judge’s bench.
rounds.answer: She swept the steps and filled the water jug on the judge’s bench.
rounds.explanation: Her role is described in one sentence, and both tasks sit side by side in it.

rounds.prompt: In part 2, what evidence did the boy of eleven give at the trial?
choices: The lesson at the end of a fable is called the moral.
He said he had seen the trader hide boxes behind the artificial wall in the storehouse.
She flew higher than any camel could reach, so from the sky she saw the thin green line behind the ridge.
rounds.answer: He said he had seen the trader hide boxes behind the artificial wall in the storehouse.
rounds.explanation: The boy gives the only direct eyewitness account in the trial, and he names the exact hiding place.

rounds.prompt: Folklore means the traditional stories and customs of a group of people. Which of these is folklore?
choices: A weather report on the radio
A shopping list on the table
A bus timetable at the station
rounds.answer: Anansi tales from West Africa
rounds.explanation: Anansi tales have been passed down through generations of storytellers, while the other three are everyday written information.

rounds.prompt: Which feature belongs to a fable rather than to a long novel?

Magic that lasts for many pages
rounds.answer: One clear problem and a short plot
rounds.explanation: A fable stays short and keeps to one problem, so nothing distracts the reader from the moral at the end.
